P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes. A Bangladesh Bank circular of 22 July 2026 eased the foreign-exchange rules for freelancers and individual service exporters. Payments can be received on electronic evidence (platform statements, emails, digital communications) instead of conventional export documents. Inward remittances up to US$20,000 can be credited without a formal declaration. Payments through online payment gateway service providers (OPGSPs) are allowed up to US$10,000 per transaction, with timely repatriation to Bangladesh required. ICT freelancers can keep up to 50% of export earnings in a foreign-currency Exporters' Retention Quota (ERQ) account; other service exporters can keep up to 30%. The rest is converted to taka.

P2_fcy_account.answer: Freelancers and service exporters can hold the retained share of export earnings in a foreign-currency Exporters' Retention Quota (ERQ) account: up to 50% for ICT freelancers, 30% for other service exporters (P1). The July 2026 circular also allows dual-currency 'freelancer cards' and wider use of mobile financial services (MFS) and payment service providers. What ERQ balances may be spent on, and general foreign-currency accounts for other residents, were not verified because the Bangladesh Bank site is blocked.

P3_local_gateways.question: Licensed local online payment gateways, and whether individuals or sole proprietors can sign up
P3_local_gateways.answer: Global platform availability for Bangladesh (automated collector snapshots, Oct 2026). Available: Paddle (not on its exclusion list; software sellers only, each seller reviewed); Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts); Polar (payouts); Whop (payouts); Dodo Payments (sellers); Google Play (developer registration); YouTube Partner Program. Not listed: Stripe (merchant sign-up); Etsy seller payments.

P3_local_gateways.notes: SSLCOMMERZ, the largest gateway, says it holds a Payment Systems Operator (PSO) licence from Bangladesh Bank. Its onboarding requirements list a sole proprietorship path (TIN, merchant enrolment form, trade licence, VAT, DBID). There is also a 'Facebook Merchant' path, which asks for contact number, email, NID and photo of the owner, a digital signature and a formal undertaking, plus DBID. That suits individuals selling via social media. Bangladesh Bank's own register of licensed PSOs/PSPs could not be read (site blocked). The licence claim is SSLCOMMERZ's own statement; the regulator's list (bb.org.bd) is blocked. Other gateways (aamarPay, shurjoPay, bKash payment gateway) were not checked.

P4_paypal.answer: PayPal does not operate in Bangladesh. Bangladesh is absent from PayPal's worldwide market list and from the PayPal Payouts eligibility table, so residents can't open PayPal accounts to receive money.

P5_payoneer_wise.question: Payoneer / Wise availability for residents
P5_payoneer_wise.answer: Payoneer: available. It has a bKash partnership with 24/7 real-time withdrawals to bKash, minimum 1,000 BDT, and no extra paperwork; local bank withdrawal is also possible. Wise: residents can't get USD account details (Bangladesh is on Wise's exclusion list) and Bangladesh isn't among the countries where you can hold money with Wise. Clients abroad can still send BDT via Wise to Bangladeshi bank accounts, bKash or Nagad.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual selling digital products or services register a business? How (sole proprietor), cost, online?
L1_registration.answer: No company registration is needed, but anyone doing digital commerce must hold an ID number. Under the Ministry of Commerce's Digital Commerce Operation Guidelines 2021 (Gazette, 4 July 2021), every individual or business doing digital commerce must obtain at least ONE of: trade licence, VAT registration, TIN, Unique Business Identification number (UBID) or Personal Retail Account (PRA) number, and display it on their marketplace or social-media page. UBID is to become mandatory in phases. A TIN (free to register online, L2) therefore meets the rule for an individual. The freelancer income-tax exemption only requires that all income, spending and investment of the business go through bank transfer (L3).

L2_tax_id.question: Tax identification number requirement and how to get it
L2_tax_id.answer: TIN (Taxpayer's Identification Number), issued by the National Board of Revenue through its online e-TIN portal (secure.incometax.gov.bd). Registration verifies your National ID / smart card number, your name as on the NID, and your date of birth, and sends an activation code to your mobile. A TIN is one of the IDs that satisfies the digital-commerce rule (L1), and SSLCOMMERZ asks for it for proprietorships (P3).

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: How residents' foreign-sourced or digital income is taxed
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Income Tax Act 2023, Sixth Schedule Part 1 paragraph 21 (authentic English text, SRO 404, Oct 2025): income of a resident or non-resident Bangladeshi individual from listed IT/digital businesses is EXEMPT from 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2027. The list includes software development, SaaS, web and app development, digital graphics design, digital animation, data entry, e-learning/e-publication, call centre and 'IT Freelancing'. All income, spending and investment of the business must go through bank transfer. The Finance Act 2026 (Gazette, 30 June 2026), section 157(b), replaced clause (q) 'IT Freelancing' with 'freelancing and content creation', widening the exemption beyond IT. Pre-budget press reports said the 7.5% source tax on foreign service receipts would also be removed for individual freelancers and content creators, and a Bangladesh Bank circular (2025) says no source tax may be deducted from IT freelancing income.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported services and digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: Standard VAT is 15% for most goods and services. VAT registration is required once annual turnover exceeds BDT 5 million. A business with turnover between BDT 3 million and BDT 5 million enlists for the 4% turnover tax instead (Kintsugi). Non-resident suppliers of digital services must register, through a local VAT agent if they have no fixed place in Bangladesh, and charge 15%.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law: name, year, in force?, regulator
L5_data_protection.answer: Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 (Act 63 of 2026), passed by Parliament on 9 April 2026 in a batch of bills adopting the interim government's ordinances. It replaced the Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025 (Ordinance 61 of 2025, gazetted 6 Nov 2025; amended 5 Feb 2026, adding real-time in-country copies for critical information infrastructure). Under the ordinance, data subjects are owners of their data and explicit consent is required. A National Data Governance Authority (created by a companion ordinance) enforces it, and some obligations start 18 months after gazette publication.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: E-commerce / consumer-protection law relevant to online sales
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Digital Commerce Operation Guidelines 2021 (Ministry of Commerce, Gazette 4 July 2021), issued under the National Digital Commerce Policy 2020 (amended) and applying across Bangladesh. Sellers on websites, marketplaces or social media must clearly state all product and service details and terms, including return and refund terms, replacement, delivery time limits and so on. Buyers must be told about cookies and special software in advance. Prior consent is needed before collecting personal data. MLM, gambling and online betting are banned. ID display rule: see L1. For physical goods, advance payment above 10% of the price is not allowed unless the product is ready to hand to a courier within 48 hours of full payment (up to 100% via a Bangladesh Bank-approved escrow). Delivery is due within 5 days in the same city or 10 days elsewhere.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; PayPal is not available. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. (6) Local official channel: Bangladesh Bank's July 2026 circular accepts electronic evidence (platform statements, emails) for freelancer receipts. You can keep up to 50% of ICT export earnings in an ERQ foreign-currency account, and Payoneer withdraws to bKash (P1/P2/P5). Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.

sources.title: Bangladesh Bank streamlines foreign exchange rules to facilitate freelancers (Jul 22, 2026)
sources.quote: In addition, freelancers in ICT sectors may retain up to 50% of their export earnings in foreign currency accounts, commonly known as Exporters’ Retention Quota (ERQ), while other service exporters may retain up to 30%, providing greater flexibility in managing international business expenses.

sources.title: Bangladesh Bank eases forex rules for freelancers (22 July 2026)
sources.quote: Freelancers in the ICT sector may retain up to 50 percent of their export earnings in foreign currency accounts, commonly known as the exporters' retention quota (ERQ), while other service exporters may retain up to 30 percent, providing flexibility in managing international business expenses.
